questions.question: Hamming distance is defined between which pair of objects?
options: Two equal-length words/vectors by counting positions that differ
Any two strings by counting insertions/deletions/substitutions
Two integers by subtracting their values
Any two byte strings by aligning them at their starts, even if lengths differ
questions.explanation: Hamming distance compares aligned positions and requires equal length; edit distance is a different concept.

questions.question: For binary vectors a and b, why is d(a,b) = weight(a XOR b) useful?
options: XOR marks exactly the positions where bits differ
XOR compresses the vectors into a shorter one
XOR sorts bits so distance is order-independent
XOR removes noise from a received word
questions.explanation: In a XOR b, a 1 means the bits differed at that position, so counting 1s gives the distance.

questions.question: What is the Hamming distance between a=101101 and b=110100?
questions.explanation: They differ in three positions (bits 2, 3, and 6).

questions.question: A common way to compute bit-level Hamming distance between equal-length byte strings is:
options: Sum popcount(x XOR y) for each pair of bytes
Count how many bytes differ (ignoring bit differences inside a byte)
Compute Levenshtein distance on their hex strings
Convert to integers and subtract, then take absolute value
questions.explanation: XOR highlights differing bits and popcount counts them; summing over bytes gives total bit distance.

questions.question: The minimum distance d_min(C) of a block code C is:
options: The minimum Hamming distance between any two distinct codewords in C
The maximum Hamming distance between any two codewords in C
The average Hamming distance between codewords in C
The distance from the all-zero word to the nearest codeword
questions.explanation: d_min looks at the closest pair of distinct valid codewords; it controls detect/correct guarantees.

questions.question: If a code has minimum distance d_min = d, what are the standard guarantees?
options: Detect up to d-1 errors; uniquely correct up to floor((d-1)/2) errors
Detect up to d errors; uniquely correct up to d-1 errors
Detect up to floor((d-1)/2) errors; uniquely correct up to d-1 errors
Detect and correct exactly d errors
questions.explanation: Detection uses the fact that < d flips can't reach another codeword; unique correction needs non-overlapping radius-t balls.

questions.question: In nearest-neighbor decoding, what does it mean if there is a tie for the closest codeword?
options: Unique decoding is not possible for that received word
The code is guaranteed to correct the error anyway
The received word must already be a valid codeword
You can safely pick either codeword without changing the message
questions.explanation: A tie means the received word lies on a decision boundary; choosing one arbitrarily can produce the wrong message.

questions.question: Attack scenario: if a system 'corrects' by breaking ties arbitrarily (e.g., first codeword wins), what can an attacker do?
options: Craft an ambiguous received word that forces a chosen decoded message (silent miscorrection)
Force the decoder to always output the all-zero codeword
Guarantee that every error will be detected and rejected
Prevent any decoding from happening at all, even for valid codewords
questions.explanation: If tie-breaking is predictable, an attacker can steer decoding outcomes by pushing words onto decision boundaries.
